At nine, Zainab opened the folder with the science project, saw the long list of steps and felt a rush of dread. Her chest tightened. She got up for a biscuit, then a quick round of the board game on the floor, and then it was dinner. The folder stayed shut. Her mother Damini put it on the table each evening without comment.

At fifteen, Zainab had a history project worth a large share of her mark. She knew exactly how to start, yet she opened the file and closed it again every night. If she began and the result was poor, everyone would see she was not as clever as they believed. Easier to wait. She told her friends, "I work best at the last minute," which sounded better than the truth.

The night before submission, she stayed up until two. The result was rushed and thin. Her teacher Suraj handed it back with a kind note: "There is a good idea in here. I would have loved to see it developed." Zainab read it twice and felt her stomach drop.

qa.q: What did Damini do with the folder each evening?
qa.a: Damini put the folder on the table each evening without comment.

qa.q: How is Zainab's reaction to her project at nine like her delay at fifteen, and how is it different?
qa.a: At nine the task feels big and dull and she moves to a biscuit and a game for quick relief, while at fifteen the task is clear but she puts it off to avoid being judged; both delay leads to weaker work.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she closed the file each night at fifteen?
qa.a: Zainab was afraid that a poor result would show she was not as clever as people believed.

qa.q: What could Zainab try at the start of the next project?
qa.a: She could share a rough first page with Suraj early, since a small start and gentle feedback make a poor result less frightening.

grounding: Procrastination linked across two ages: a child moving to something easier when a task feels big, and a teenager delaying a project to avoid judgement of a poor result.

passage:
At sixteen, Omkar had a geography project and a whole month to finish it. He kept saying, "I'll begin on Saturday." If he tried and the map came out crooked, his teacher would see that he was not good at this. Doing nothing kept the picture of himself intact. The night before, he pasted a rushed collage and got a weak mark.

At twenty-five, at his first office job, Omkar noticed the same heavy feeling as a report deadline crept closer. This time he closed the game he had opened and asked himself, "What exactly is uncomfortable? Is it that I'm scared it won't be good? Is it that I don't know the first step? Or is it just dull?" He wrote the answer on a sticky note: "I don't know what the client wants."

He turned to his colleague Varun. "Can I ask you two questions about the brief?" Varun nodded, and the fog began to lift.

qa.q: What did Omkar write on his sticky note?
qa.a: He wrote, "I don't know what the client wants."

qa.q: What has changed in how Omkar handles delay between sixteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: At sixteen he avoids starting to protect his image, and the work suffers; at twenty-five he asks what exactly is uncomfortable, names the real feeling as unclear steps, and asks Varun for help.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he put off the geography map at sixteen?
qa.a: Omkar was afraid of looking bad, since a crooked map might show his teacher he was not good at it.

qa.q: Why did naming the feeling help Omkar at twenty-five?
qa.a: Naming it as not knowing what the client wanted separated the feeling from the whole task and pointed to a fix, asking Varun about the brief.

grounding: Procrastination linked across ages: a teenager avoiding a project for fear of judgement, and a young professional naming the real feeling behind delay and asking for help.

passage:
At sixteen, Sunaina saw a cyclone warning flash on her phone while she was scrolling in bed. "It never comes here," she told her brother. Nothing bad had ever happened in their street, so she swiped the alert away and watched another video. The storm turned out to be weaker than forecast, and she felt she had been right.

At twenty, living in a ground-floor flat by the river, Sunaina heard another warning, and her neighbour Nilesh knocked to say the road might flood. Earlier warnings had passed with little damage, so she shrugged and stayed put. By evening water was creeping under the door. When it reached the sofa, the road to the main gate was already a brown stream.

Nilesh called from the first-floor landing. "Come up now. I've called the emergency number." Sunaina grabbed her documents and phone, waded through ankle-deep water and climbed the stairs. From the balcony they watched a rescue boat move slowly down the lane.

qa.q: Where was Sunaina living at twenty?
qa.a: She was living in a ground-floor flat by the river.

qa.q: How does Sunaina's thinking at sixteen lead to her situation at twenty?
qa.a: At sixteen nothing had ever happened, so she felt safe and swiped the alert away; at twenty earlier warnings that passed make her wait until the water reaches her sofa and the road is cut, showing how feeling that it cannot happen here delays leaving.

qa.q: What was Sunaina probably feeling at sixteen when her prediction seemed right?
qa.a: Sunaina felt reassured and even proud that she had been right to ignore the warning, which strengthened her confidence that nothing bad happens here.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that protected Sunaina?
qa.a: Nilesh warned her early, called the emergency number and told her to come upstairs, which got her to a safer floor before the water rose further.

grounding: Normalcy bias across ages: a teenager dismissing a warning because nothing has happened before, and the same person later waiting too long during a flood.

passage:
At ten, Santosh threw his maths paper on the desk. "Miss gave me low marks because she was in a bad mood," he said. "It's just luck. Anyone can get lucky." His mother Parveen asked whether he had done the practice sums. "Why bother?" he shrugged. "It doesn't change anything." He slid the paper into his bag and stopped opening the workbook.

At fifteen, after failing a physics test, Santosh sat with his friend Wasim by the tea stall. He was upset, but he took out a pen. "What can I actually control today?" he asked, and wrote on a napkin: "Redo the chapter problems. Ask sir about the wrong ones." Wasim said, "And what about the things you can't control?" "The paper, the results day, all that. I'll accept that and get on with the rest," Santosh said.

That evening he solved twelve problems and felt steadier, though the result remained uncertain.

qa.q: What did Santosh blame for his low maths marks at ten?
qa.a: He blamed the teacher's bad mood and luck.

qa.q: How does Santosh's way of explaining results at ten differ from his way at fifteen?
qa.a: At ten he says the low marks come from luck or the teacher's mood, so he sees no point in effort; at fifteen he asks what he can control today, takes one action on it and accepts what he cannot change.

qa.q: What was Santosh probably feeling when he said "Why bother?" to his mother?
qa.a: Santosh felt discouraged and powerless, believing that effort would not change the outcome.

qa.q: What did Wasim's question add to Santosh's plan?
qa.a: Wasim's question about what he cannot control led Santosh to separate his own part from the rest, which keeps hope without self-blame.

grounding: Locus of control across two ages: a child who attributes marks to luck or the teacher's mood, and a teenager who asks what is within his control and acts on it.

passage:
Eight-year-old Sharmila had a notebook of riddles and a reputation to match. "What has hands but cannot clap?" she asked her friend Rashmi at lunch. "A clock!" Rashmi cried. They groaned over a pun about tomatoes ("You say tomato, I say to-marry-o") and waved at anyone who passed. Sharmila loved the wordplay and the way it made the group laugh together.

The following month, during reading time, she stumbled over the word "enormous" and the class snickered. Her face flushed. Before anyone could speak, she stretched her arms wide and boomed, "E-NOR-MOUSE!" with a squeak. The room broke into laughter again, and Sharmila grinned, in charge of it.

At the end of the day her teacher Gurpreet said quietly, "That was quick thinking. Did the stumble bother you? We can practise the hard words on Thursdays if you like." Sharmila picked at her sleeve and said, "Maybe. Just a bit."

qa.q: What did Sharmila ask Rashmi at lunch?
qa.a: She asked, "What has hands but cannot clap?"

qa.q: How does Sharmila's humour with riddles differ from her joke about enormous?
qa.a: Sharmila's riddles and puns make the whole group laugh together over wordplay; after stumbling on "enormous" she stretches her arms wide and booms "E-NOR-MOUSE!" so the class laughs again and she is in charge of the moment, though she admits it bothered her a bit.

qa.q: What was Sharmila probably feeling when her face flushed at the class snicker?
qa.a: Sharmila felt embarrassed and put on the spot, which pushed her to turn the moment into a joke.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do that helped Sharmila?
qa.a: Gurpreet praised the quick thinking, asked gently whether the stumble bothered her, and offered practice with hard words on Thursdays.

grounding: Two uses of humour by the same child: wordplay and riddles that share fun with friends, and a joke told to take control after a reading stumble.

passage:
Five-year-old Lakshmi lay upside down on the sofa. "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the phone?" Her mother Binita sat down and set out paper and crayons without a lecture. "Try a picture of the whole street," she said. Lakshmi grumbled, then began drawing the mango tree with a very long trunk. She was still colouring when dinner came.

Four years later, Lakshmi heard her father Nilesh sigh loudly over his laptop and huff at his tea. She froze in the doorway. Was he tired of her? Had she done something wrong? She hovered, then asked, "Papa, is everything fine?"

Nilesh rubbed his neck and laughed a little. "Oh! That sigh had nothing to do with you. The internet has been slow all afternoon, and I'm relieved it finally works." He patted the sofa. "Thanks for asking. Want to draw with me?" Lakshmi's shoulders dropped and she went to find the crayons.

qa.q: What did Binita set out for Lakshmi when she said she was bored?
qa.a: Binita set out paper and crayons.

qa.q: What ties Lakshmi's boredom at five to her worry over her father's sigh at nine?
qa.a: At five Lakshmi lies upside down on the sofa saying she is bored, and Binita sets out paper and crayons; at nine she freezes when her father Nilesh sighs and huffs, wondering whether she caused it, until she asks and he explains. A restless mood and a sigh are both easy to misread until someone checks.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling as she froze in the doorway at her father's sigh?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt worried and unsure, afraid that she had done something wrong.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that eased Lakshmi's worry?
qa.a: Nilesh explained that the sigh was about the slow internet, thanked her for asking, and invited her to draw with him.

grounding: Boredom in a young child settled by simple materials, and the same child later misreading an adult's sigh until she asks.
